title: King's Indian: the main line move by move, with reasons
outcomes: Plays the Classical main line (6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7 9.Ne1 Nd7 10.Be3 f5 11.f3 f4 12.Bf2 g5) and says what each move prepares
Names the natural-looking moves that fail (Nxe5, ...Nxe4, Bxa7, ...Nd4) and counts attackers and defenders before capturing
Explains why White plays c5 on the queenside while Black plays on the kingside, and names the move that supports each lever
Reads opening counts as results of games, not verdicts, and knows the sidelines 7...exd4, 8.dxe5 and 8.Be3

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Classical main line runs about twelve moves, and almost every move has a reason. steps.text: **What 8...Ne7 prepares.** The knight leaves c6 with a purpose: from e7 it covers g6 and f5, the squares Black needs for the pawn advance that follows [I]. The pawn on d5 locks the centre, so the wings decide: White plays on the queenside, Black on the kingside. [H] That is why this structure is easy to describe and hard to play.

steps.text: **Two plans, one race.** White opens the queenside with c5, supported by a knight on d3 or a pawn on b4. Black opens the kingside with f5, f4 and g5, supported by the knights. Neither side can stop the other's plan cheaply. [H] The side that keeps its king safe and times its lever correctly wins the race; the moves above show the timing in outline, not as a rule.

**Why each side plays on its own wing.** In a locked centre the only pawns that can still move are on the wings. A lever is a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn. White's lever is c4-c5, which attacks d6, supported by Nd3 or b4. Black's lever is ...f5, which attacks e4, supported by the knights, and later ...f4 and ...g5. Each lever opens lines toward the other side's king or pieces. [I]

steps.text: **Reading the counts.** In our master file the pawn push to d5 is played in 629 of 730 games, the ninth-move pawn lever in 307 of 613, the knight retreat to d7 in 140 of 196. A count says what strong players chose, not why and not whether it is best. We checked each main move with the engine at depth 16 and found it close to the best; that checks the move, not the crowd.

**One feature at a time.** Three positions, one question: is the capture on e4 safe? In the first the white knight is back on b1. The second is the main line. In the third a white a-pawn has moved one square. Predict each before you open it.
steps.chapter: Test yourself and teach it back

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** White builds, castles and locks the centre with a pawn on d5; the attacked knight retreats to e7 with a purpose. Both sides then clear a path for a pawn: the white knight leaves f3, the black knight leaves f6. White supports the c-pawn lever, Black pushes three pawns on the kingside, and the attacked bishop retreats to f2. Count before capturing: three natural captures in this line each lose a piece. Counts show choices, not verdicts.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in two or three sentences, explain to a beginner why White plays on the queenside and Black on the kingside in this line. Say when the plan works, when it fails, give one example you could set up on a board, and one mistake to avoid. Self-check: did I say when it works and fails, give an example, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.
